title: Backpropagating Pauli Propagation
authors: Sheng-Hsuan Lin, Etienne Granet, Kevin Hémery, Henrik Dreyer
abstract: We develop a backpropagation algorithm for evaluating parameter gradients in quantum circuits using Pauli propagation simulation. The method has computational complexity comparable to that of standard sparse Pauli simulation techniques, while producing gradients whose accuracy is of the same order as the corresponding observable expectation values. By exploiting the reversibility of quantum circuits, the algorithm reduces the memory cost by a factor of $\mathcal{O}(n_\text{param})$ compared with conventional reverse-mode automatic differentiation, where $n_\text{param}$ denotes the number of parameters in the circuit. Compared with finite difference methods, the algorithm is $\mathcal{O}(n_\text{param})$ more efficient in function evaluations. These features enable efficient and accurate classical optimization of quantum circuits for applications such as state preparation and time-evolution compression, while also allowing operator-complexity measures such as the operator stabilizer Rényi entropy to be monitored and regularized during optimization. We demonstrate the method by optimizing low-energy state-preparation circuits for transverse-field Ising models in one, two, and three dimensions and for the three-dimensional Heisenberg model, and by compressing two-dimensional time-evolution circuits.
summary: This paper introduces an efficient backpropagation algorithm tailored for calculating gradients in quantum circuits simulated using Pauli propagation. By exploiting circuit reversibility, it achieves significant memory savings compared to standard automatic differentiation techniques. This enables accurate and scalable classical optimization of quantum models relevant to condensed matter physics.
main_problem: The primary goal is developing a memory-efficient backpropagation algorithm to calculate parameter gradients for quantum circuits simulated via Pauli propagation.
main_result: The proposed method achieves computational complexity comparable to standard sparse Pauli simulation while offering significant memory savings ($\mathcal{O}(n_{	ext{param}})$) over conventional reverse-mode automatic differentiation.
method: It employs a specialized backpropagation technique that exploits the reversibility of quantum circuits, allowing gradient calculation by recomputing intermediate operators rather than storing them all.
model_or_system: The work focuses on simulating quantum circuits applied to models like the transverse-field Ising model and the Heisenberg model, which are relevant in condensed matter physics.
key_observables: Parameter gradients ($\partial L / \partial 	heta$), observable expectation values, and operator-complexity measures such as the operator stabilizer Rényi entropy.
important_parameters: The number of parameters ($n_{	ext{param}}$) in the circuit is crucial for determining computational scaling and memory savings.
main_assumptions: The method relies on finite truncation thresholds ($\delta$) during Pauli propagation, which introduces controlled errors; it also assumes the cost function depends only on the final layer's observable state.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the forward (Heisenberg updates) and backward (gradient calculation) propagation workflow. Figure 2 compares norm error and operator infidelity between forward and backward passes, showing consistency with the truncation threshold $\delta$.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem of gradient computation in Pauli simulation, details the forward pass using Heisenberg evolution rules for observables, presents the novel memory-efficient reverse-mode algorithm utilizing circuit reversibility, and validates it by applying it to state preparation and time-evolution compression tasks.
why_interesting: This work provides a crucial computational tool for optimizing quantum circuits applied to condensed matter models (like Ising/Heisenberg), enabling efficient parameter tuning that was previously limited by memory constraints in gradient estimation.

Instead, we utilize the reversibility of the quantum circuit and recompute the values on the nodes on the fly in the backward pass.
